''Trumbull'', 1888. [Maryland.]

'''whifflery''' (hwif′lėr-i), ''n.'' The characteristics or habits of a whiffler; trifling; levity.
{{smaller block|Life is no frivolity, or hypothetical coquetry or ''whifflery.''
{{right|''Carlyle'', in Froude, Life in London, iii.}}}}

'''whiffletree''' (hwif′l-trē), ''n.'' [< ''whiffle'', turn, + ''tree.'' Cf. ''whippletree'', ''swingletree.''] Same as ''swingletree.''

'''whift''' (hwift), ''n.'' [Var. of ''whiff''<sup>1</sup>.] A whiff or waft; a breath; a snatch. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|A sweep of lutestrings, laughs, and ''whifts'' of song.
{{right|''Browning'', Fra Lippo Lippi.}}}}

'''whig<sup>1</sup>''' (hwig), ''n.'' '''1.''' Sour whey. ''Brockett.'' [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>With green cheese, clouted cream, with flawns and custard stor’d,
''Whig'', cyder, and with whey, I domineer a lord.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Muses’ Elysium, vi.}}
<poem>Drinke ''Whig'' and sowre Milke, whilest I rince my Throat
With Burdeaux and Canarie.</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', English Traveller (ed. Pearson), i. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' Buttermilk. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''whig<sup>2</sup>''' (hwig), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''whigged'', ppr. ''whigging.'' [Cf. Sc. ''whiggle'', var. of ''wiggle:'' see ''wiggle.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To move at an easy and steady pace; jog. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The Solemn League and Covenant
Came ''whigging'' up the hills, man.</poem>
{{right|''Battle of Killiecrankie'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 155).}}}}
'''To whig awa’ wi’''', to drive briskly on with. ''Jamieson.''
{{smaller block|I remember hearing a Highland farmer in Eskdale, after giving minute directions to those who drove the hearse of his wife how they were to cross some boggy land, conclude, “Now, lads, ''whig awa’ wi’'' her.”
{{right|''Scott.'' (''Jamieson.'')}}}}

¶
'''whiggery''' (hwig′ėr-i), ''n.'' [< ''whig''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ery.''] The principles or practices of Whigs: first applied to the Scottish Presbyterian doctrine, and generally used as a term of contempt.

{{RunningHeader|whiff|6898|whiggery}}To puff; blow; produce or emit a puff or whiff. {{smaller block|When through their green boughs ''whiffing'' winds do whirl,
With wanton pufs their wauing locks to curl. {{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 2.}}}} '''2.''' To drink. [Prov. Eng.] '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To puff; puff out; exhale; blow: as, to ''whiff'' out rings of smoke.—'''2.''' To carry as by a slight blast or whiff of wind. {{smaller block|Old Empedocles’s way, who, when he leapt into Ætna, having a dry sear body, and light, the smoke took him and ''whift'' him up into the moon. {{right|''B. Jonson'', World in the Moon.}}}} {{smaller block|How was it scornfully ''whiffed'' aside! {{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., I. v. 2.}}}} '''3†.''' To draw in; imbibe; inhale: said of air or smoke, and frequently of liquids also. {{smaller block|Every skull And skip-iacke now will have his pipe of smoke, And ''whiff'' it bravely till hee ’s like to choke. {{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 71.}}}} {{smaller block|In this season we might press and make the wine, and in winter ''whiff'' it up. {{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, i. 27.}}}} '''whiff'''2 (hwif), ''n.''   [Origin obscure.]   An anacanthine or malacopterygious fish of the family ''Pleuronectidæ'', a kind of flatfish or flounder, the ''Cynicoglossus microcephalus'', found in British waters; the smear-dab, sail-fluke, or mary-sole. '''whiff'''3 (hwif), ''v. i.''   [An error for ''whip'', ''v. i.'', 2.]   To fish, as for mackerel, with a hand-line. See ''whiffing'', ''n.'' {{smaller block|One might as well argue that, because bits of red flannel or of tobacco-pipe are highly successful baits in ''whiffing'' for Mackerel, therefore these substances form a “favourite food” of this fish. {{right|''Nature'', XLI. 538.}}}} '''whiffer''' (hwif′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''whiff''1 + ''-er''1.]   One who whiffs. {{smaller block|Great tobacco-''whiffers'';
They would go near to rob with a pipe in their mouths. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Wit at Several Weapons, iv. 1.}}}} '''whiffet''' (hwif′et), ''n.''   [< ''whiff''1 + ''-et''1.]   '''1.''' A little whiff.   ''Imp. Dict.'' [Rare.]—'''2.''' A whipper-snapper; a whipster; any insignificant or worthless person. [U. S.] {{smaller block|The sneaks, ''whiffets'', and surface rats. {{right|''Philadelphia Times'', Aug. 1, 1883.}}}} '''whiffing''' (hwif′ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''whiff''3, ''v.'']   '''1.''' Surface-fishing with a hand-line. {{smaller block|''Whiffing'', the process of slowly towing the bait (sculling or pulling in the known haunts of the fish). {{right|''Field'', Dec. 26, 1885. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}} {{smaller block|It [the whiting] is often caught by ''whiffing'', when it gives good sport. {{right|''Stand. Nat. Hist.'', III. 273.}}}} '''2.''' A kind of hand-line used for taking mackerel, pollack, and the like. '''whiffing-tackle''' (hwif′ing-tak″l), ''n.'' The tackle used in whiffing; surface-tackle. '''whiffle''' (hwif′l), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''whiffled'', ppr. ''whiffling''.   [Freq. of ''whiff''1; perhaps confused with D. ''weifelen'', waver.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To blow in gusts; hence, to veer about, as the wind. {{smaller block|Two days before this storm began, the Wind ''whiffled'' about to the South, and back again to the East, and blew very faintly. {{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, II. iii. 66.}}}} {{smaller block|Seizing a shovel, he went by the back door to the front of the house, at a spot where the ''whiffling'' winds had left the earth nearly bare [of snow], and commenced his subnivean work. {{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 17.}}}} '''2.''' To change from one opinion or course to another; use evasions; prevaricate; be fickle or unsteady; waver. {{smaller block|A person of a ''whiffling'' and unsteady turn of mind, who cannot keep close to a point of a controversy. {{right|''Watts'', Improvement of the Mind, I. ix. § 27.}}}} '''3.''' To trifle; talk idly.   ''Phillips'', 1706;   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] {{smaller block|I am not like those officious and importunate sots who, by force, outrage, and violence, constrain an easy, good-natured fellow to ''whiffle'', quaff, carouse, and what is worse. {{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, iii., Prol.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To disperse with a puff; blow away; scatter. {{smaller block|Such as would ''whiffle'' away all these truths by resolving them into a mere moral allegory. {{right|''Dr. H. More'', Epistles to the Seven Churches, ix.}} {{right|[(''Latham.'')}}}} '''2.''' To cause to change, as from one opinion or course to another. {{smaller block|Every man ought to be stedfast and unmovable in them [the main things of religion], and not suffer himself to be ''whiffled'' out of them by an insignificant noise about the infallibility of a visible church. {{right|''Tillotson'', Sermons, lxv.}}}} '''3.''' To shake or wave quickly. ''Donne.'' '''whiffle†''' (hwif′l), ''n.''   [< ''whiffle'', ''v.'', in sense of orig. verb.]   A fife. {{smaller block|Whiffler, . . . one that plays on a ''Whiffle'' or Fife. {{right|''Bailey'', 1727.}}}} '''whiffler''' (hwif′lėr), ''n.''   [< ''whiffle'' + ''-er''1.]   '''1†.''' A piper or fifer. {{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', On Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}} '''2†.''' A herald or usher; a person who leads the way, or prepares the way, for another: probably so called because the pipers (see ''piper''1, 1) usually led the procession. {{smaller block|The deep-mouth’d sea, Which like a mighty ''whiffler'' ’fore the king Seems to prepare his way. {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., v., cho., l. 12.}}}} {{smaller block|The term [whiffler] is undoubtedly borrowed from whiffle, another name for a fife or small flute; for ''whifflers'' were originally those who preceded armies or processions as fifers or pipers. ''F. Douce'', Illus. of Shakespeare, p. 311. I can go in no corner but I meet with some of my ''whifflers'' in their accoutrements. {{right|''Chapman'', Monsieur D’Olive, iii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''Whiflers'' of your inferior and Chiefe companies cleere the wayes before him. {{right|''Dekker'', Seven Deadly Sins, p. 43.}}}} {{smaller block|Before the dame, and round about, March’d ''whifflers'' and staffiers on foot. {{right|''S. Butler'', Hudibras, II. ii. 650.}}}} '''3.''' One who whiffles; one who changes frequently his opinion or course; one who uses shifts and evasions in argument; a fickle or unsteady person. {{smaller block|Your right ''whiffler'' indeed hangs himself in Saint Martin’s, and not in Cheapside. {{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Every ''whiffler'' in a laced coat . . . shall talk of the constitution. {{right|''Swift.''}}}} '''4.''' A puffer of tobacco; a whiffer. ''Halliwell.''—'''5.''' The whistlewing, or goldeneye duck. ''G. Trumbull'', 1888. [Maryland.] '''whifflery''' (hwif′lėr-i), ''n.'' The characteristics or habits of a whiffler; trifling; levity. {{smaller block|Life is no frivolity, or hypothetical coquetry or ''whifflery.'' {{right|''Carlyle'', in Froude, Life in London, iii.}}}} '''whiffletree''' (hwif′l-trē), ''n.''   [< ''whiffle'', turn, + ''tree.'' Cf. ''whippletree'', ''swingletree.'']   Same as ''swingletree.'' '''whift''' (hwift), ''n.''   [Var. of ''whiff''1.]   A whiff or waft; a breath; a snatch. [Rare.] {{smaller block|A sweep of lutestrings, laughs, and ''whifts'' of song. {{right|''Browning'', Fra Lippo Lippi.}}}} '''whig1''' (hwig), ''n.'' '''1.''' Sour whey. ''Brockett.'' [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.] {{smaller block|With green cheese, clouted cream, with flawns and custard stor’d, ''Whig'', cyder, and with whey, I domineer a lord. {{right|''Drayton'', Muses’ Elysium, vi.}}}} {{smaller block|Drinke ''Whig'' and sowre Milke, whilest I rince my Throat With Burdeaux and Canarie. {{right|''Heywood'', English Traveller (ed. Pearson), i. 2.}}}} '''2.''' Buttermilk. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] '''whig2''' (hwig), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''whigged'', ppr. ''whigging.''   [Cf. Sc. ''whiggle'', var. of ''wiggle:'' see ''wiggle.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To move at an easy and steady pace; jog. [Scotch.] {{smaller block|The Solemn League and Covenant Came ''whigging'' up the hills, man. {{right|''Battle of Killiecrankie'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 155).}}}} '''To whig awa’ wi’''', to drive briskly on with. ''Jamieson.'' {{smaller block|I remember hearing a Highland farmer in Eskdale, after giving minute directions to those who drove the hearse of his wife how they were to cross some boggy land, conclude, “Now, lads, ''whig awa’ wi’'' her.” {{right|''Scott.'' (''Jamieson.'')}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' To urge forward, as a horse. [Scotch.] '''whig3''' (hwig), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Formerly also ''whigg''; prob. short for ''whiggamore'', q. v.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One of the adherents of the Presbyterian cause in Scotland about the middle of the seventeenth century: a name given in derision. {{smaller block|When in the teeth they dar’d our ''Whigs'', An’ covenant true blues, man. {{right|''Burns'', Battle of Sheriff-Muir.}}}} {{smaller block|I doubt I’ll hae to tak the hills wi’ the wild ''whigs'', as they ca’ them, and . . . be shot down like a mawkin at some dyke-side. {{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, vii.}}}} '''2.''' [''cap.''] A member of one of the two great political parties of Great Britain, the other being the Tories (later the Conservatives). {{smaller|The Whigs were the successors of the Roundheads of the Civil War and the Country party of the Restoration. The name was given to them about 1679 as a reproach by their opponents, the Court party, through a desire to confound them with the rebel Whigs of Scotland (see ''whig''3, 1). The Whigs favored the Revolution of 1688-9, and governed Great Britain for a long period in the eighteenth century. In general, they may be called the party of progress; one of their principal achievements was the passage of the Reform Bill in 1832. About the same time the name ''Whig'' began to be replaced by ''Liberal'', though still retained to denote the more conservative members of the Liberal party. See ''Liberal'', ''Tory''.}} {{smaller block|The south-west counties of Scotland have seldom corn enough to serve them round the year: And . . . those in the west come in the summer to buy at Leith the stores that come from the north: And from a word, Whiggam, used in driving their horses, all that drove were called the Whiggamors, and shorter the Whigs. Now in that year, inburgh. And they came up marching on the head of their parishes, with an unheard-of fury, praying and preaching all the way as they came. The Marquis of Argile and his party came and headed them, they being about 6,000. This was called the Whiggamor’s inroad. And ever after that all that opposed the Court came in contempt to be called ''Whiggs.'' And from Scotland the word was brought into England, where it is now one of our unhappy terms of distinction. {{right|''Bp. Burnet'', Hist. Own Times, I. 58.}}}} {{smaller block|I hate a ''Whig'' so much that I’ll throw my Husband out of his Election, or throw myself out of the World! a Parcel of canting Rogues; they have always Moderation in their Mouths—rank Resistance in their Hearts—and hate Obedience even to their lawful Wives. {{right|''Mrs. Centlivre'', Gotham Election, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|The prejudice of the Tory is for establishment; the prejudice of the ''Whig'' is for innovation. A Tory does not wish to give more real power to Government, but that Government should have more reverence. Then they differ as to the Church. The Tory is not for giving more legal power to the Clergy, but wishes they should have a considerable influence, founded on the opinion of mankind; the ''Whig'' is for limiting and watching them with a narrow jealousy. {{right|''Johnson'', in Boswell, an. 1781.}}}} '''3.''' [''cap.''] In ''Amer. hist.'': (''a'') A member of the patriotic party during the revolutionary period. {{smaller block|The Hessians and other foreigners, looking upon that as the right of war, plunder wherever they go, from both ''Whigs'' and Tories, without distinction. {{right|''Robert Morris'', Dec. 21, 1776, quoted in Lecky’s Eng. in [18th Cent., xiv.}}}} (''b'') One of a political party in the United States which grew up, in opposition to the Democratic party, out of the National Republican party. {{smaller block|It was first called the Whig party in 1834. Its original principles were extension of nationalizing tendencies, and support of the United States Bank, of a protective tariff, and of a system of internal improvements at national expense. It won the presidential elections of 1840 and 1848, but soon after divided upon the slavery question. It lost its last national election in 1852, and soon after many of its members became temporarily members of the American and Constitutional Union parties, but eventually most of its northern members became Republicans, most of its southern members Democrats.—'''Conscience-Whig''', in ''U. S. hist.'', in the last days of the Whig party, one of those northern Whigs who were indisposed to regard the compromise of 1850 as a final settlement of the slavery question: so called from their conscientious objections to such compromises with slavery.—'''Cotton-Whig''', in ''U. S. hist.'', in the last days of the Whig party, one of those northern Whigs who were disposed to regard the compromise of 1850 as a final settlement of the slavery question: so called from their supposed partiality to the cotton interest.}} '''II.''' ''a.'' Relating to or composed of Whigs, in any use of that word; whiggish: as, ''Whig'' measures; a ''Whig'' ministry. {{smaller block|The hope that America would supply the main materials for the suppression of the revolt [the American Revolution] proved wholly chimerical. One of the first acts of the ''Whig'' party in every colony was to disarm Tories. {{right|''Lecky'', Eng. in 18th Cent., xiv.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''Whig'' party was always opposed to slavery. But there was a broad and well-understood distinction between Whig opponents of slavery and the fanatical Abolitionists. {{right|''T. W. Barnes'', Thurlow Weed, p. 306.}}}} '''whig4''' (hwig), ''n.'' A variant of ''wig''2. [North. Eng. and Scotch.] {{smaller block|A cook whose recipes were hopelessly old-fashioned, and who had an exasperating belief in the sufficiency of buttered ''whigs'' and home-made marmalade for all requirements. {{right|''Mrs. Humphry Ward'', Robert Elsmere, ii.}}}} '''whiggamore''' (hwig′ạ-mōr), ''n.''   [Also ''whiggamor'', ''whigamore''; according to Burnet, derived from ''whiggam'', as used by the men orig. called ''whiggamores'' (def. 1) in driving their horses; ''whiggam'' is a dubious word, appar. connected with ''whig''2, jog: see ''whig''2. In the glossary to the Waverley novels ''whigamore'' is defined “a great whig,” appar. implying a derivation < ''whig''3 + Gael. ''mor'', great; whereas the evidence indicates that ''whig''3 is an abbr. of ''whiggamore''. No Gael. form that could be the base of ''whiggamore'' appears; but it may be a perverted form from an original not now obvious.]   '''1.''' A person who came from the west and southwest of Scotland to Leith to buy corn. See the quotation from Bishop Burnet, under ''Whig''3, 2.—'''2.''' One of the people of the west of Scotland who marched to Edinburgh in 1648, their expedition being called the ''whiggamores’ inroad'' (see the quotation referred to in def. 1). Hence—'''3.''' A Scotch Presbyterian; one of the party opposed to the court; a whig. {{smaller block|There [at Bothwell Brigg] was he and that sour ''whigamore'' they ca’d Burley. {{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, xxxvii.}}}} '''whiggarchy''' (hwig′är-ki), ''n.''   [< ''whig''3 + Gr. ἀρχειν, rule.]   Government by Whigs. [Rare.] {{smaller block|They will not recognise any other government in Great Britain but ''whiggarchy'' only. {{right|''Swift'', App. to Conduct of the Allies.}}}} '''whiggery''' (hwig′ėr-i), ''n.''   [< ''whig''3 + ''-ery.'']   The principles or practices of Whigs: first applied to the Scottish Presbyterian doctrine, and generally used as a term of contempt.
